chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
title: Why Mingus bands were inimitable; amateurs versus great soloists
summary: Mingus says others copied his arrangements and pedal points, and that his ensemble sound outstripped his soloists.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah, he did. I've noticed something, that we were talking about imitations before we did the interview, which I loved. We were talking about People who could do imitations of Erroll Garner, whatever. But one of the things I've noticed about your music is that it may have influenced a lot of people. I know it did. I mean, a lot of people learned a lot from that music, but that it was virtually inimitable, that nobody -- it's just not possible for somebody else to sit down and get a band to sound the way you do. And maybe you feel differently about that. But --
I think some guys made their bands -- they caught my style in arrangements. Miles Davis, Max Roach, with an extended chord and pedal points.
I'm not saying they didn't steal from you. Everybody stole from you. I'm talking about getting the band to sound the way you did. Your bands always had so much fire and energy.

Yeah, because I had amateur musicians. I never used the guys who -- yes, I did, I had Ernie Henry Hiemann one time, I had one of the best. It was at a time he was playing good, too. I never had guys like Benny Bailey or Ernie Henry Hiemann at the same time in the band. Always got a sound ensemble that would play, but solos were never up to par with what the arrangements were.
